subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling (latency/concurrency/burst) — next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Evan Thompson <evan@nimbusretail.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-15T14:05:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling (latency/concurrency/burst) — next steps

Hi Evan — thanks again for your time earlier. Quick recap from our call on performance SLOs and autoscaling so we have alignment and clear next steps.

Summary of your targets (as stated on call):
- 95th-pct end-to-end latency for interactive chat (streaming token-by-token) <= 250 ms for single-turn prompts; target <= 300 ms for multi-turn sessions with a 3-turn context.
- Sustained throughput: 200 concurrent active sessions (steady-state).
- Burst tolerance: tolerate spikes up to 750 concurrent sessions for up to ~5 minutes with graceful degradation.
- Streaming requirements: first token emitted within 120–150 ms; subsequent tokens streamed at real-time rates.
- Availability SLO: 99.9% for production traffic; need visibility into cold-starts and scaling events.

Key notes on autoscaling / burst behavior we discussed:
- Warm pool approach: we recommend keeping a small warm pool (pre-warmed GPU slots) to reduce cold-starts for expected bursts. Warm pool instances route in <5s vs cold node adds ~45–90s depending on instance type and region.
- Scale-up rate: autoscaler can add capacity at ~10 nodes/min under current config; per-node concurrent streaming capacity ~20 sessions (depends on model size & sequence length).
- Queueing: short queueing (recommended 30–60s) before returning 429/503 to calling app; we can configure prioritized queues for high-priority traffic.
- Fallbacks: automatic model-variant fallback to lower-cost / lower-latency quantized variants if we detect sustained overload.

Immediate next steps we proposed on the call:
1) You to confirm anticipated QPS/burst profile (typical day + peak).
2) We’ll schedule a 2-hour load test (staging) — Dylan to lead technical plan.
3) Send over your security/POC access requirements; we’ll share a pre-auth checklist.
4) Draft runbook entries for queueing/backpressure and SLA behavior to share with your infra team.

Attached is the perf targets sheet we started filling out during the call. I’ll loop Dylan for the technical plan and Ben for pricing/commits.

Thanks — talk soon.

—
Marissa Cole

Subject: Re: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling (latency/concurrency/burst) — next steps

Marissa — thanks for the summary, this is helpful. A few clarifications before we schedule the load test: 

- Concurrency: when you say 200 concurrent sessions sustained, that’s concurrently active streaming sessions across the fleet, correct? Our users open multiple tabs sometimes; should we plan per-user concurrency of ~2–3?
- Burst profile: the 750 sessions burst is a conservative upper bound — typical peak we expect ~400–500 for a marketing push. Can Redwood handle 750 for short windows without impacting 95th-pct for existing users?
- Cold starts: the 45–90s number is scary for user experience. Is the warm pool something we can configure to be larger during anticipated campaigns? What’s the cost implication?
- Queueing: prefer graceful degradation over a hard 429 for premium users — can we prioritize?

Also can you confirm whether streaming first-token time (120–150 ms) is typical for the 7B-class model you showed? Our initial plan is to start on a 7B quantized variant.

If you can loop in Dylan with a proposed load test plan and toggles for warm pool + prioritized queueing, we can pick dates next week.

—Evan
Evan Thompson
Head of Product, Nimbus Retail
evan@nimbusretail.com
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling (latency/concurrency/burst) — next steps

Evan — great questions, answered inline and looping Dylan/Ben for technical/pricing specifics.

- Concurrency: yes — 200 refers to active streaming sessions across the fleet. If you expect per-user concurrency of 2–3, we’ll account for that in the load profile.
- Burst handling: we can tolerate short bursts to 750 by combining warm pool + short queuing + prioritized routing. Sustained beyond a few minutes will degrade 95th-pct unless additional reserved capacity is provisioned.
- Warm pool sizing: absolutely configurable. During campaigns we can increase pre-warmed slots for the window (auto-schedule or manual). Cost impact is additive for the pre-warmed capacity; Ben will include a delta estimate in the pricing.
- Priority queues: yes — we offer prioritized queues so premium traffic is drained ahead of lower-priority requests. When queue limits are reached we return 429 for low-priority and try to keep premium traffic.
- First-token time: for a 7B quantized variant in our hosted environment we typically see first-token in the 100–160 ms range (region dependent). The numbers I quoted earlier were conservative.

Dylan — can you propose a 2-hour staging load-test plan (config, expected metrics, failure modes to exercise, warm pool sizes to try)? Also include our measurement points: 50/90/95/99 pcts for token latency, first-byte latency, tail-response, and per-node concurrency.

Ben — please prepare quick pricing delta for: increase warm pool from baseline to +50 and +200 slots for a 2-hour window, and an estimate for reserved capacity if they want guaranteed headroom.

Evan — once Dylan posts the plan we’ll propose Wed/Thu next week for the run.

—Marissa

On Tue, Mar 16, 2026 at 9:45 AM Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com> wrote:
> Dylan — can you propose a 2-hour staging load-test plan ...

Summary plan (high level) — staging load test (2 hours):
1) Test objectives:
   - Validate 95th/99th-pct E2E latency under steady-state and burst conditions
   - Measure scale-up time and impact on tail latency during node add events
   - Validate prioritized queueing behavior and failure modes

2) Staging environment config:
   - Model: 7B quantized variant (same weights/config as PoC)
   - Baseline capacity: 10 nodes (per-node concurrent streaming sessions ~= 20) -> baseline ~200 concurrent sessions
   - Warm pool settings to test: 0 (cold), 25, 100, 200 pre-warmed slots
   - Autoscaler config: default scale rate 10 nodes/min (we’ll also simulate a slower ramp to measure impacts)

3) Traffic profile:
   - Steady phase: ramp to 200 concurrent sessions over 10 min, sustain 40 min
   - Burst phase: synthetic spike to 500 sessions for 5 minutes, then to 750 for 2 minutes
   - Multi-tab per-user simulation: include 2x per-user concurrency in some cohorts

4) Measurement points / metrics:
   - First-token latency (ms) 50/90/95/99 pct
   - Inter-token streaming rate (tokens/sec) and token emission jitter
   - End-to-end response time per request (incl. queuing) 50/90/95/99 pct
   - Queue depth and drop counts (429s returned) by priority tier
   - Node provisioning time (time between scale decision and node available for routing)
   - CPU/GPU utilization, memory, and KV-cache hit rates

5) Failure modes to exercise:
   - Cold starts with 0 warm pool
   - Rapid repeated small bursts vs single large burst
   - Node failures during bursts to validate fallback to model variants

6) Acceptance criteria (examples):
   - 95th-pct first-token <= 250 ms during steady-state for premium tier
   - Tail latencies during bursts do not violate premium SLO more than X% of requests (to be agreed)

7) Logistics:
   - Need a staging access window (2 hours) and an endpoint for our load driver to hit (we’ll provide auth tokens).
   - Please provide expected QPS and representative prompt sizes (avg tokens per request and context length).

I will produce a runnable script and a dashboard for the run. Post-test we’ll generate a runbook with recommended warm-pool sizing and autoscaler params for production.

—Dylan
